nodes.name: General $Y\in\mathcal{S}^p$

Hence, in order to prove Formula \eqref{diffenrential}, we have to show that $\xi$ has a limit in $0$ and that $$ \underset{t 	o 0}{\lim} \ \xi(t) = n \left[\Gamma^{A, \ldots, A}(f^{[n]}) ight](K, \ldots, K) \ \ 	ext{in} \ \ \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H}). $$ For any $1\leq k\leq n$ and any $t\in \mathbb{R}$, let $\Gamma_k(t) = \Gamma^{(A+tZ)^{n-k+1}, (A)^k}(f^{[n]}).$ Since $K = i[A,Y] + Z$, we have, for any $1\leq k \leq n$,  egin{align*} \left[\Gamma_k(t) ight](K,\ldots,K) & = \left[ \Gamma_k(t) ight] (Z, \ldots, Z) \ & + \sum_{j=1}^n \ \sum_{\substack{K_m = i[A,Y] \	ext{or} \ K_m=Z, \ 1 \leq m \leq n-1}} i \left[ \Gamma_k(t) ight] (K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, [A,Y], K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1}) \end{align*} Hence,  egin{align*} \xi(t) & = \sum_{k=1}^{n} \left[ \Gamma_k(t) ight] (Z, \ldots, Z) \ & + \sum_{k=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^n \ \sum_{\substack{K_m = i[A,Y] \	ext{or} \ K_m=Z, \ 1 \leq m \leq n-1}} i \left[ \Gamma_k(t) ight] (K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, [A,Y], K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1}). \end{align*} By Lemma $ef{simplification5}$ and Lemma $ef{MOIcomm}$ we have  egin{align*} \sum_{k=1}^{n} \left[ \Gamma_k(t) ight] (Z, \ldots, Z) & = \dfrac{1}{t} \left[ \Gamma^{A+tZ,\ldots, A+tZ}(f^{[n-1]}) - \Gamma^{A,\ldots, A}(f^{[n-1]}) ight](Z, \ldots, Z) \ & = \dfrac{1}{(n-1)!} \ \dfrac{f^{(n-1)}(A+tZ)-f^{(n-1)}(A) }{t} \ Z^{n-1}. \end{align*} By \cite[Lemma 3.4 (ii)]{KS}, this quantity converges as $t$ goes to $0$ in $\mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$ to $$ \dfrac{1}{(n-1)!} \ f^{(n)}(A) Z^n. $$ Since $n! f^{[n]}(x,\ldots,x) = f^{(n)}(x)$, the latter is in turn, by Lemma $ef{MOIcomm}$, equal to $$ n \left[\Gamma^{A,\ldots, A}(f^{[n]}) ight](Z, \ldots, Z). $$ We will now show that for any $1\leq j,k \leq n$ and for any $K_1, \ldots, K_{n-1}$ with $K_m= Z$ or $i[A,Z]$, $1\leq m \leq n-1$, $$ \left[\Gamma_k(t)ight](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, [A,Y], K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1}) $$ goes to $\left[\Gamma^{A,\ldots, A}(f^{[n]}) ight](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, [A,Y], K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1})$ in $\mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$ as $t$ goes to $0$. Assume first that $n-k+2 \leq j \leq n$. Since $A$ and $Z$ are bounded operators, we have, by Remark $ef{approximatebdd}$,  egin{align*} & \left[\Gamma_k(t)ight](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, [A,Y], K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1}) \ & = \left[\Gamma^{(A+tZ)^{n-k+1},(A)^{k-1}}(f^{[n-1]}) ight](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, YK_j, K_{j+1}, \ldots, K_{n-1}) \ & \ \ \ - \left[\Gamma^{(A+tZ)^{n-k+1},(A)^{k-1}}(f^{[n-1]}) ight](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, YK_{j-1}, K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1}), \end{align*} with a simple modification in the case $j=n$. By Lemma $ef{simplification5}$ the latter converges, as $t$ goes to $0$, to  egin{align*} &\left[\Gamma^{A, \ldots, A}(f^{[n-1]}) ight](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, YK_j, K_{j+1}, \ldots, K_{n-1}) \ & - \left[\Gamma^{A, \ldots, A}(f^{[n-1]}) ight](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, YK_{j-1}, K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1}), \end{align*} which is in turn equal to $\left[\Gamma^{A,\ldots, A}(f^{[n]}) ight](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, [A,Y], K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1})$. Assume now that $j=n-k+1$. In this case, by Remark $ef{approximatebdd}$,  egin{align*} & \left[\Gamma^{(A+tZ)^{n-k+1},(A)^k}(f^{[n]}) ight](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, (A+tZ)Y - YA, K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1}) \ & = \left[\Gamma^{(A+tZ)^{n-k+1},(A)^{k-1}}(f^{[n-1]}) ight](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, YK_j, K_{j+1}, \ldots, K_{n-1}) \ & \ \ \ - \left[\Gamma^{(A+tZ)^{n-k+1},(A)^{k-1}}(f^{[n-1]}) ight](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, YK_{j-1}, K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1}). \end{align*} Since $(A+tZ)Y - YA = [A,Y] +tZY$, we get  egin{align*} & \left[\Gamma_k(t)ight](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, [A,Y], K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1}) \ & = \left[\Gamma^{(A+tZ)^{n-k+1},(A)^{k-1}}(f^{[n-1]}) ight](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, YK_j, K_{j+1}, \ldots, K_{n-1}) \ & \ \ \ - \left[\Gamma^{(A+tZ)^{n-k+1},(A)^{k-1}}(f^{[n-1]}) ight](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, YK_{j-1}, K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1}) \ & \ \ \ - t \left[\Gamma^{(A+tZ)^{n-k+1},(A)^k}(f^{[n]}) ight](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, ZY, K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1}). \end{align*} The inequality  egin{align*} & \| t \left[\Gamma^{(A+tZ)^{n-k+1},(A)^k}(f^{[n]}) ight](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, ZY, K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1}) \|_p \ & \leq |t| c_{p,n} \|f^{(n)}\|_{\infty} \|K_1\|_p \ldots \|K_{n-1}\|_p \|ZY\|_p \end{align*} and the same reasoning as for the case $n-k+2 \leq j \leq n$ show that $$ \left[\Gamma_k(t)ight](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, [A,Y], K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1}) $$ converges to $\left[\Gamma^{A,\ldots, A}(f^{[n]}) ight](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, [A,Y], K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1})$. Finally, assume that $1\leq j \leq n-k$. By Remark $ef{approximatebdd}$,  egin{align*} & \left[\Gamma^{(A+tZ)^{n-k+1},(A)^k}(f^{[n]}) ight](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, [A+tZ,Y], K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1}) \ & = \left[\Gamma^{(A+tZ)^{n-k+1},(A)^{k-1}}(f^{[n-1]}) ight](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, YK_j, K_{j+1}, \ldots, K_{n-1}) \ & \ \ \ - \left[\Gamma^{(A+tZ)^{n-k+1},(A)^{k-1}}(f^{[n-1]}) ight](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, YK_{j-1}, K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1}), \end{align*} with a simple modification in the case $j=1$ as in Remark $ef{approximatebdd}$. Note that $[A+tZ,Y] = [A,Y] + t[Z,Y]$ and then reason as in the previous case to show that $$ \left[\Gamma_k(t)ight](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, [A,Y], K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1}) $$ goes to $\left[\Gamma^{A,\ldots, A}(f^{[n]}) ight](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, [A,Y], K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1})$ in $\mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$ as $t$ goes to $0$. Hence, we proved that  egin{align*} & \underset{t 	o 0}{\lim} \ \xi(t) \ & = n \left[\Gamma^{A,\ldots, A}(f^{[n]}) ight](Z, \ldots, Z) \ & \ \ \ \ + \sum_{k=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n \ \sum_{\substack{K_m = i[A,Y] \	ext{or} \ K_m=Z, \ 1 \leq m \leq n-1}} i \left[ \Gamma^{A, \ldots, A}(f^{[n]}) ight] (K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, [A,Y], K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1}) \ & = n \left[\Gamma^{A,\ldots, A}(f^{[n]}) ight](K, \ldots, K). \end{align*} This proves that $\varphi \in D^n(\mathbb{R},\Sc^p(\H))$ and that for any $1\leq k \leq n$, $\varphi^{(k)}$ is given by \eqref{diffenrential}. Finally, let $I\subset \mathbb{R}$ be a bounded interval and let $1 \leq i \leq n-1$. We let $J \subset \mathbb{R}$ to be a bounded interval such that, for any $t\in I$, $\sigma(A+tK) \subset J$. There exists $f_i \in C^i(\mathbb{R})$ compactly supported such that $f_i = f$ on $J$. Then for any $t\in I$,  egin{align*} \dfrac{1}{k!} \varphi^{(i)}(t) & = \left[ \Gamma^{A+tK, A+tK, \ldots, A+tK}((f^{[i]})_{|J^{n+1}}) ight] (K, \ldots, K) \ & = \left[ \Gamma^{A+tK, A+tK, \ldots, A+tK}(f_i^{[i]}) ight] (K, \ldots, K). \end{align*} Hence, since $f_i^{(i)}$ is bounded on $\mathbb{R}$, $\varphi^{(i)}$ is bounded on $I$ by Theorem $ef{BddnessMOI}$. Similarly, since $f^{(n)}$ is bounded on $\mathbb{R}$, $\varphi^{(n)}$ is bounded on $\mathbb{R}$.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $n$: reduce differentiability at $0$ to a dense set of $K=i[A,Y]+Z$ (Lemma 3.7), replace $A+tK$ by the unitary path $\nu(t)$ (Lemma 3.8), and compute the limit of $\xi(t)$ term by term with Lemmas 3.5, 3.6 and Remark 2.9.

nodes.name: Base case $n=1$
nodes.statement: The assumptions on $f$ ensure, by \cite[Theorem 7.13]{KPSS}, that $\varphi$ is differentiable on $\mathbb{R}$ and that for any $t\in \mathbb{R}$, $$ \varphi'(t) = \left[\Gamma^{A+tK, A+tK}(f^{[1]}) \right](K). $$
nodes.statement_short: The first derivative is given by KPSS as a double operator integral of $f^{[1]}$.

nodes.name: Induction hypothesis and target
nodes.statement: Assume now that $\varphi$ is $(n-1)$-times differentiable on $\mathbb{R}$ with $$ \dfrac{\varphi^{(n-1)}(t)}{(n-1)!} = \left[\Gamma^{A+tK, \ldots, A+tK}(f^{[n-1]}) \right](K, \ldots, K). $$ We have to show that the function $$ \psi : t\in \mathbb{R} \mapsto \left[\Gamma^{A+tK, \ldots, A+tK}(f^{[n-1]}) \right](K, \ldots, K) $$ is differentiable and that for any $t\in \mathbb{R}$, $$ \psi'(t) = n \left[\Gamma^{A+tK, \ldots, A+tK}(f^{[n]}) \right](K, \ldots, K). $$
nodes.statement_short: Assume the formula at order $n-1$ and reduce to differentiability of $\psi$ with $\psi'(t)=n[\Gamma(f^{[n]})](K,\ldots,K)$.

nodes.name: Reduce to $t=0$ and to a dense set
nodes.statement: It is clear that we only have to prove the differentiability in $0$, from which we can deduce the differentiabily on $\mathbb{R}$. In this case, by Lemma $\ref{simplification3}$, it is sufficient to prove the differentiability for $K$ belonging to a dense subset of $(\mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H}))_{\text{sa}}$. By \cite[Proposition 6.2]{KPSS}, the subspace $X_0$ defined by $$ X_0 = \left\lbrace i[A,Y] + Z \ \text{with} \ Y,Z \in (\mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H}))_{\text{sa}} \ \text{and} \ Z \ \text{commutes with} \ A \right\rbrace \subset (\mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H}))_{\text{sa}} $$ is dense in $(\mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H}))_{\text{sa}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 3.7 lets us restrict to the dense subspace $X_0=\{i[A,Y]+Z\}$ of KPSS.

nodes.name: Fix $K=i[A,Y]+Z$
nodes.statement: Let $K = i[A,Y] + Z \in X_0$ and show that $$ \psi_0 : t\in \mathbb{R} \mapsto \left[\Gamma^{A+tK, \ldots A+tK}(f^{[n-1]}) \right](K, \ldots, K) $$ is differentiable in $0$ with $$ \psi_0'(0) = n \left[\Gamma^{A, \ldots, A}(f^{[n]}) \right](K, \ldots, K). $$
nodes.statement_short: State the goal $\psi_0'(0)=n[\Gamma^{A,\ldots,A}(f^{[n]})](K,\ldots,K)$ for such $K$.

nodes.name: Pass to the unitary path $\nu(t)$
nodes.statement:
Let $
u(t) = e^{-itY}(A+tZ)e^{itY}$. We have $
u(0)=A$ and $
u$ is $\mathcal{S}^p$-differentiable in $0$ with $
u'(0)=K$. Hence, by Lemma $ef{simplification4}$, to prove the latter, it is equivalent to prove that $	ilde{\psi} : \mathbb{R} 	o \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$ defined by $$ 	ilde{\psi}(t) = \left[ \Gamma^{
u(t),\ldots,
u(t)}(f^{[n-1]}) ight](K, \ldots, K), t\in \mathbb{R}, $$ is differentiable in $0$ with $$ 	ilde{\psi}'(0) = n \left[\Gamma^{A, \ldots, A}(f^{[n]}) ight](K, \ldots, K). $$
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 3.8 replaces $A+tK$ by $\nu(t)=e^{-itY}(A+tZ)e^{itY}$.

nodes.name: Expand the difference quotient
nodes.statement_short: Proposition 2.8 turns $\frac{\tilde\psi(t)-\tilde\psi(0)}{t}$ into a sum of $f^{[n]}$-integrals with slot $\frac{\nu(t)-A}{t}$.

nodes.name: Conjugation identity
nodes.statement:
Note that  egin{align*} & \left[ \Gamma^{(
u(t))^{n-k+1}, (A)^k}(f^{[n]})ight]\left( K,\ldots,K ight) \ & \ \ \ \ \ \ = e^{-itY}\left[ \Gamma^{(A+tZ)^{n-k+1}, (A)^k}(f^{[n]})ight]\left((e^{itY}Ke^{-itY})^{n-k},e^{itY}K, (K)^{k-1} ight). \end{align*} In fact, more generally, for any $t\in \mathbb{R}$, for any $g\in 	ext{Bor}(\mathbb{R}^{n+1})$ such that $\Gamma^{(
u(t))^{n-k+1}, (A)^k}(g) \in \mathcal{B}_n(\mathcal{S}^p)$ and any $X \in \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$, we have  egin{align*} & \left[ \Gamma^{(
u(t))^{n-k+1}, (A)^k}(g)ight]\left(X, \ldots, X ight) \ & \ \ \ \ \ \ = e^{-itY}\left[ \Gamma^{(A+tZ)^{n-k+1}, (A)^k}(g)ight]\left((e^{itY}Xe^{-itY})^{n-k},e^{itY}X, (X)^{k-1} ight). \end{align*} Indeed, when $g$ is an element of $	ext{Bor}(\mathbb{R}) \otimes \cdots \otimes 	ext{Bor}(\mathbb{R})$, this equality is a consequence of the fact that for any $h \in 	ext{Bor}(\mathbb{R})$, $h(e^{-itY}(A+tZ)e^{itY}) = e^{-itY}h(A+tZ)e^{itY}$. Hence, if $p=2$, the general case follows from the $w^*$-continuity of multiple operator integrals. If $1<p<\infty$, we approximate $X\in \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$ by elements of $\mathcal{S}^2(\mathcal{H}) \cap \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$. Details are left to the reader.
nodes.statement_short: Conjugating by $e^{itY}$ moves $\nu(t)$ back to $A+tZ$; proved on tensor symbols and extended by $w^*$-continuity and density.

nodes.name: Remove the conjugation in the limit
nodes.statement: Now, when $t$ goes to $0$, $e^{-itY} \to 1$ in $\mathcal{B}(\mathcal{H})$ so that $e^{itY}Ke^{-itY}, e^{itY}K \to K$ in $\mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$. Hence, by uniform boundedness of $\Gamma^{(A+tZ)^{n-k+1}, (A)^k}(f^{[n]}) \in \mathcal{B}_n(\mathcal{S}^p), t\in \mathbb{R}$, we have that if one of those limits exists, so does the second one and then \begin{align*} & ~ \ \ \ \underset{t \to 0}{\lim} \ e^{-itY}\left[ \Gamma^{(A+tZ)^{n-k+1}, (A)^k}(f^{[n]})\right]\left((e^{itY}Ke^{-itY})^{n-k},e^{itY}K, (K)^{k-1} \right) \\ & = \underset{t \to 0}{\lim} \ \left[ \Gamma^{(A+tZ)^{n-k+1}, (A)^k}(f^{[n]})\right]\left(K, \ldots, K \right). \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: As $t\to0$ the conjugated arguments converge, so the two limits coincide.

nodes.name: Reduce to the limit of $\xi(t)$
nodes.statement: Define $$ \xi(t) = \displaystyle \sum_{k=1}^n \left[ \Gamma^{(A+tZ)^{n-k+1}, (A)^k}(f^{[n]})\right] (K, \ldots, K), t \in \mathbb{R}. $$ The latter implies that if $\xi$ has a limit in $0$, then so does $\dfrac{\tilde{\psi}(t) - \tilde{\psi}(0)}{t}$ with the same limit. Hence, in order to prove Formula \eqref{diffenrential}, we have to show that $\xi$ has a limit in $0$ and that $$ \underset{t \to 0}{\lim} \ \xi(t) = n \left[\Gamma^{A, \ldots, A}(f^{[n]}) \right](K, \ldots, K) \ \ \text{in} \ \ \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H}). $$
nodes.statement_short: It remains to show $\xi(t)\to n[\Gamma^{A,\ldots,A}(f^{[n]})](K,\ldots,K)$.

nodes.name: Expand $K=i[A,Y]+Z$ multilinearly
nodes.statement: For any $1\leq k\leq n$ and any $t\in \mathbb{R}$, let $\Gamma_k(t) = \Gamma^{(A+tZ)^{n-k+1}, (A)^k}(f^{[n]}).$ Since $K = i[A,Y] + Z$, we have, for any $1\leq k \leq n$, \begin{align*} \left[\Gamma_k(t) \right](K,\ldots,K) & = \left[ \Gamma_k(t) \right] (Z, \ldots, Z) \\ & + \sum_{j=1}^n \ \sum_{\substack{K_m = i[A,Y] \\\text{or} \ K_m=Z, \\ 1 \leq m \leq n-1}} i \left[ \Gamma_k(t) \right] (K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, [A,Y], K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1}) \end{align*} Hence, \begin{align*} \xi(t) & = \sum_{k=1}^{n} \left[ \Gamma_k(t) \right] (Z, \ldots, Z) \\ & + \sum_{k=1}^{n} \sum_{j=1}^n \ \sum_{\substack{K_m = i[A,Y] \\\text{or} \ K_m=Z, \\ 1 \leq m \leq n-1}} i \left[ \Gamma_k(t) \right] (K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, [A,Y], K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1}). \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Split each $\Gamma_k(t)(K,\ldots,K)$ into the pure $Z$ term and terms containing one commutator $[A,Y]$.

nodes.name: The pure $Z$ term
nodes.statement: By Lemma $\ref{simplification5}$ and Lemma $\ref{MOIcomm}$ we have \begin{align*} \sum_{k=1}^{n} \left[ \Gamma_k(t) \right] (Z, \ldots, Z) & = \dfrac{1}{t} \left[ \Gamma^{A+tZ,\ldots, A+tZ}(f^{[n-1]}) - \Gamma^{A,\ldots, A}(f^{[n-1]}) \right](Z, \ldots, Z) \\ & = \dfrac{1}{(n-1)!} \ \dfrac{f^{(n-1)}(A+tZ)-f^{(n-1)}(A) }{t} \ Z^{n-1}. \end{align*} By \cite[Lemma 3.4 (ii)]{KS}, this quantity converges as $t$ goes to $0$ in $\mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$ to $$ \dfrac{1}{(n-1)!} \ f^{(n)}(A) Z^n. $$ Since $n! f^{[n]}(x,\ldots,x) = f^{(n)}(x)$, the latter is in turn, by Lemma $\ref{MOIcomm}$, equal to $$ n \left[\Gamma^{A,\ldots, A}(f^{[n]}) \right](Z, \ldots, Z). $$
nodes.statement_short: Lemmas 3.6 and 3.5 identify the $Z$-term with a difference quotient of $f^{(n-1)}(A+tZ)$, converging to $n[\Gamma^{A,\ldots,A}(f^{[n]})](Z,\ldots,Z)$.

nodes.name: Reduce the commutator terms
nodes.statement: We will now show that for any $1\leq j,k \leq n$ and for any $K_1, \ldots, K_{n-1}$ with $K_m= Z$ or $i[A,Z]$, $1\leq m \leq n-1$, $$ \left[\Gamma_k(t)\right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, [A,Y], K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1}) $$ goes to $\left[\Gamma^{A,\ldots, A}(f^{[n]}) \right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, [A,Y], K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1})$ in $\mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$ as $t$ goes to $0$.
nodes.statement_short: State the claim that each commutator term converges to the corresponding $\Gamma^{A,\ldots,A}$ term.

nodes.name: Case $n-k+2 \le j \le n$
nodes.statement: Assume first that $n-k+2 \leq j \leq n$. Since $A$ and $Z$ are bounded operators, we have, by Remark $\ref{approximatebdd}$, \begin{align*} & \left[\Gamma_k(t)\right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, [A,Y], K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1}) \\ & = \left[\Gamma^{(A+tZ)^{n-k+1},(A)^{k-1}}(f^{[n-1]}) \right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, YK_j, K_{j+1}, \ldots, K_{n-1}) \\ & \ \ \ - \left[\Gamma^{(A+tZ)^{n-k+1},(A)^{k-1}}(f^{[n-1]}) \right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, YK_{j-1}, K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1}), \end{align*} with a simple modification in the case $j=n$. By Lemma $\ref{simplification5}$ the latter converges, as $t$ goes to $0$, to \begin{align*} &\left[\Gamma^{A, \ldots, A}(f^{[n-1]}) \right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, YK_j, K_{j+1}, \ldots, K_{n-1}) \\ & - \left[\Gamma^{A, \ldots, A}(f^{[n-1]}) \right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, YK_{j-1}, K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1}), \end{align*} which is in turn equal to $\left[\Gamma^{A,\ldots, A}(f^{[n]}) \right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, [A,Y], K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1})$.
nodes.statement_short: Remark 2.9 rewrites the commutator slot as a difference of two $f^{[n-1]}$-integrals, and Lemma 3.6 gives the limit.

nodes.name: Case $j=n-k+1$
nodes.statement: Assume now that $j=n-k+1$. In this case, by Remark $\ref{approximatebdd}$, \begin{align*} & \left[\Gamma^{(A+tZ)^{n-k+1},(A)^k}(f^{[n]}) \right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, (A+tZ)Y - YA, K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1}) \\ & = \left[\Gamma^{(A+tZ)^{n-k+1},(A)^{k-1}}(f^{[n-1]}) \right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, YK_j, K_{j+1}, \ldots, K_{n-1}) \\ & \ \ \ - \left[\Gamma^{(A+tZ)^{n-k+1},(A)^{k-1}}(f^{[n-1]}) \right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, YK_{j-1}, K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1}). \end{align*} Since $(A+tZ)Y - YA = [A,Y] +tZY$, we get \begin{align*} & \left[\Gamma_k(t)\right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, [A,Y], K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1}) \\ & = \left[\Gamma^{(A+tZ)^{n-k+1},(A)^{k-1}}(f^{[n-1]}) \right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, YK_j, K_{j+1}, \ldots, K_{n-1}) \\ & \ \ \ - \left[\Gamma^{(A+tZ)^{n-k+1},(A)^{k-1}}(f^{[n-1]}) \right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, YK_{j-1}, K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1}) \\ & \ \ \ - t \left[\Gamma^{(A+tZ)^{n-k+1},(A)^k}(f^{[n]}) \right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, ZY, K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1}). \end{align*} The inequality \begin{align*} & \| t \left[\Gamma^{(A+tZ)^{n-k+1},(A)^k}(f^{[n]}) \right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, ZY, K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1}) \|_p \\ & \leq |t| c_{p,n} \|f^{(n)}\|_{\infty} \|K_1\|_p \ldots \|K_{n-1}\|_p \|ZY\|_p \end{align*} and the same reasoning as for the case $n-k+2 \leq j \leq n$ show that $$ \left[\Gamma_k(t)\right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, [A,Y], K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1}) $$ converges to $\left[\Gamma^{A,\ldots, A}(f^{[n]}) \right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, [A,Y], K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1})$.
nodes.statement_short: Here $(A+tZ)Y-YA=[A,Y]+tZY$, so an extra $O(t)$ term appears and vanishes in the limit.

nodes.name: Case $1 \le j \le n-k$ and conclusion
nodes.statement: Finally, assume that $1\leq j \leq n-k$. By Remark $\ref{approximatebdd}$, \begin{align*} & \left[\Gamma^{(A+tZ)^{n-k+1},(A)^k}(f^{[n]}) \right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, [A+tZ,Y], K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1}) \\ & = \left[\Gamma^{(A+tZ)^{n-k+1},(A)^{k-1}}(f^{[n-1]}) \right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, YK_j, K_{j+1}, \ldots, K_{n-1}) \\ & \ \ \ - \left[\Gamma^{(A+tZ)^{n-k+1},(A)^{k-1}}(f^{[n-1]}) \right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, YK_{j-1}, K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1}), \end{align*} with a simple modification in the case $j=1$ as in Remark $\ref{approximatebdd}$. Note that $[A+tZ,Y] = [A,Y] + t[Z,Y]$ and then reason as in the previous case to show that $$ \left[\Gamma_k(t)\right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, [A,Y], K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1}) $$ goes to $\left[\Gamma^{A,\ldots, A}(f^{[n]}) \right](K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, [A,Y], K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1})$ in $\mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$ as $t$ goes to $0$. Hence, we proved that \begin{align*} & \underset{t \to 0}{\lim} \ \xi(t) \\ & = n \left[\Gamma^{A,\ldots, A}(f^{[n]}) \right](Z, \ldots, Z) \\ & \ \ \ \ + \sum_{k=1}^n \sum_{j=1}^n \ \sum_{\substack{K_m = i[A,Y] \\\text{or} \ K_m=Z, \\ 1 \leq m \leq n-1}} i \left[ \Gamma^{A, \ldots, A}(f^{[n]}) \right] (K_1, \ldots, K_{j-1}, [A,Y], K_j, \ldots, K_{n-1}) \\ & = n \left[\Gamma^{A,\ldots, A}(f^{[n]}) \right](K, \ldots, K). \end{align*} This proves that $\varphi \in D^n(\mathbb{R},\Sc^p(\H))$ and that for any $1\leq k \leq n$, $\varphi^{(k)}$ is given by \eqref{diffenrential}.
nodes.statement_short: Using $[A+tZ,Y]=[A,Y]+t[Z,Y]$ the same reasoning applies, giving $\lim_{t\to0}\xi(t)=n[\Gamma^{A,\ldots,A}(f^{[n]})](K,\ldots,K)$.

nodes.name: Boundedness of the derivatives
nodes.statement: Finally, let $I\subset \mathbb{R}$ be a bounded interval and let $1 \leq i \leq n-1$. We let $J \subset \mathbb{R}$ to be a bounded interval such that, for any $t\in I$, $\sigma(A+tK) \subset J$. There exists $f_i \in C^i(\mathbb{R})$ compactly supported such that $f_i = f$ on $J$. Then for any $t\in I$, \begin{align*} \dfrac{1}{k!} \varphi^{(i)}(t) & = \left[ \Gamma^{A+tK, A+tK, \ldots, A+tK}((f^{[i]})_{|J^{n+1}}) \right] (K, \ldots, K) \\ & = \left[ \Gamma^{A+tK, A+tK, \ldots, A+tK}(f_i^{[i]}) \right] (K, \ldots, K). \end{align*} Hence, since $f_i^{(i)}$ is bounded on $\mathbb{R}$, $\varphi^{(i)}$ is bounded on $I$ by Theorem $\ref{BddnessMOI}$. Similarly, since $f^{(n)}$ is bounded on $\mathbb{R}$, $\varphi^{(n)}$ is bounded on $\mathbb{R}$.
nodes.statement_short: Replace $f$ by a compactly supported $f_i$ agreeing on a bounded spectral window; Theorem 2.7 then bounds $\varphi^{(i)}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.2
nodes.statement: By \cite[Theorem 7.18]{KPSS}, $\varphi$ is differentiable on $\mathbb{R}$ and for any $t\in \mathbb{R}$, $\varphi'(t) = \left[\Gamma^{A+tK, A+tK}(f^{[1]}) \right](K).$ Assume now that $\varphi$ is $(n-1)$-times differentiable on $\mathbb{R}$ with $$ \dfrac{\varphi^{(n-1)}(t)}{(n-1)!} = \left[\Gamma^{A+tK, \ldots, A+tK}(f^{[n-1]}) \right](K, \ldots, K). $$ We will prove that the function $$ \psi : t\in \mathbb{R} \mapsto \left[\Gamma^{A+tK, \ldots, A+tK}(f^{[n-1]}) \right](K, \ldots, K) $$ is differentiable in $0$ and that \begin{equation} \psi'(0) = n \left[\Gamma^{A, \ldots, A}(f^{[n]}) \right](K, \ldots, K). \end{equation} For any $m\geq 1$, let $E_m = \chi_{[-m,m]}(A)$. Then $A_m := AE_m$ is bounded. Note that $(E_m)_{m\geq 1}$ converges strongly to the identity so for any $K\in \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$, $K_m:=E_m K E_m$ converges to $K$ in $\mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$ as $m$ goes to $\infty$. This implies that the set $$ X_0 = \left\lbrace K_m \ | \ K \in (\mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H}))_{\text{sa}}, m\geq 1 \right\rbrace \subset (\mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H}))_{\text{sa}} $$ is dense in $(\mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H}))_{\text{sa}}$. Hence, by Lemma $\ref{simplification3}$, we only have to prove \eqref{unbbproof} for $K$ element of $X_0$. Let $K=K_m \in X_0$ for some $m\geq 1$. By Lemma $\ref{reducbdd}$, we have, for any $t\in \mathbb{R}$, $$ \psi(t) = \left[\Gamma^{A_m+tK_m, \ldots, A_m+tK_m}(f^{[n-1]}) \right](K_m, \ldots, K_m) $$ which is, by Theorem $\ref{FormulaSA}$, differentiable in $0$ with $$ \psi'(0) = n\left[\Gamma^{A_m, \ldots, A_m}(f^{[n]}) \right](K_m, \ldots, K_m). $$ Using Lemma $\ref{reducbdd}$ again, we see that $$ \psi'(0) = n\left[\Gamma^{A, \ldots, A}(f^{[n]}) \right](K_m, \ldots, K_m). $$ This proves that $\varphi \in D^n(\mathbb{R},\Sc^p(\H))$ and that the derivatives of $\varphi$ are given by \eqref{diffenrentialunbdd}. Finally, the boundedness of the derivatives follows from Theorem $\ref{BddnessMOI}$.
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $n$ again: the compressions $K_m=E_mKE_m$ form a dense set, Lemma 3.9 replaces $A$ by the bounded $A_m$, and Theorem 3.1 applies.

nodes.name: Base case $n=1$
nodes.statement: By \cite[Theorem 7.18]{KPSS}, $\varphi$ is differentiable on $\mathbb{R}$ and for any $t\in \mathbb{R}$, $\varphi'(t) = \left[\Gamma^{A+tK, A+tK}(f^{[1]}) \right](K).$
nodes.statement_short: KPSS gives the first derivative in the unbounded case.

nodes.name: Induction hypothesis and target
nodes.statement: Assume now that $\varphi$ is $(n-1)$-times differentiable on $\mathbb{R}$ with $$ \dfrac{\varphi^{(n-1)}(t)}{(n-1)!} = \left[\Gamma^{A+tK, \ldots, A+tK}(f^{[n-1]}) \right](K, \ldots, K). $$ We will prove that the function $$ \psi : t\in \mathbb{R} \mapsto \left[\Gamma^{A+tK, \ldots, A+tK}(f^{[n-1]}) \right](K, \ldots, K) $$ is differentiable in $0$ and that \begin{equation} \psi'(0) = n \left[\Gamma^{A, \ldots, A}(f^{[n]}) \right](K, \ldots, K). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Assume order $n-1$ and reduce to $\psi'(0)=n[\Gamma^{A,\ldots,A}(f^{[n]})](K,\ldots,K)$.

nodes.name: The dense set of compressions
nodes.statement: For any $m\geq 1$, let $E_m = \chi_{[-m,m]}(A)$. Then $A_m := AE_m$ is bounded. Note that $(E_m)_{m\geq 1}$ converges strongly to the identity so for any $K\in \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$, $K_m:=E_m K E_m$ converges to $K$ in $\mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$ as $m$ goes to $\infty$. This implies that the set $$ X_0 = \left\lbrace K_m \ | \ K \in (\mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H}))_{\text{sa}}, m\geq 1 \right\rbrace \subset (\mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H}))_{\text{sa}} $$ is dense in $(\mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H}))_{\text{sa}}$.
nodes.statement_short: $X_0=\{E_mKE_m\}$ is dense in $(\mathcal{S}^p)_{\rm sa}$ since $E_m\to 1$ strongly.

nodes.name: Reduce to bounded $A_m$ and apply Theorem 3.1
nodes.statement: Hence, by Lemma $\ref{simplification3}$, we only have to prove \eqref{unbbproof} for $K$ element of $X_0$. Let $K=K_m \in X_0$ for some $m\geq 1$. By Lemma $\ref{reducbdd}$, we have, for any $t\in \mathbb{R}$, $$ \psi(t) = \left[\Gamma^{A_m+tK_m, \ldots, A_m+tK_m}(f^{[n-1]}) \right](K_m, \ldots, K_m) $$ which is, by Theorem $\ref{FormulaSA}$, differentiable in $0$ with $$ \psi'(0) = n\left[\Gamma^{A_m, \ldots, A_m}(f^{[n]}) \right](K_m, \ldots, K_m). $$
nodes.statement_short: Lemma 3.9 rewrites $\psi$ with the bounded $A_m$, so Theorem 3.1 gives differentiability at $0$.

nodes.name: Return to $A$
nodes.statement: Using Lemma $\ref{reducbdd}$ again, we see that $$ \psi'(0) = n\left[\Gamma^{A, \ldots, A}(f^{[n]}) \right](K_m, \ldots, K_m). $$ This proves that $\varphi \in D^n(\mathbb{R},\Sc^p(\H))$ and that the derivatives of $\varphi$ are given by \eqref{diffenrentialunbdd}.
nodes.statement_short: A second application of Lemma 3.9 restores $A$ in the derivative formula.

nodes.name: Boundedness of the derivatives
nodes.statement: Finally, the boundedness of the derivatives follows from Theorem $\ref{BddnessMOI}$.
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 2.7 bounds each $\varphi^{(k)}$ on all of $\mathbb{R}$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.3
nodes.statement: The existence of the derivatives $\displaystyle \frac{d^k}{dt^k}\Big(f(A+tK)\Big)\Big|_{t=0}, k=1, \ldots, n-1,$ are ensured by Theorem $\ref{FormulaSA}$ and Theorem $\ref{FormulaSAunbdd}$. The representation \eqref{Taylor} can be obtained by induction on $n$, using Theorem $\ref{BddnessMOI}$. See the proof of \cite[Theorem 4.1 (ii)]{CLSS} for more details. From this representation, we obtain the estimate \eqref{Taylorineq} by applying Inequality \eqref{IneqDDn}.
nodes.statement_short: Existence of the derivatives comes from Theorems 3.1-3.2, the representation by induction on $n$ as in CLSS, and the estimate by applying inequality (2.9).

nodes.name: Existence of the derivatives
nodes.statement: The existence of the derivatives $\displaystyle \frac{d^k}{dt^k}\Big(f(A+tK)\Big)\Big|_{t=0}, k=1, \ldots, n-1,$ are ensured by Theorem $\ref{FormulaSA}$ and Theorem $\ref{FormulaSAunbdd}$.
nodes.statement_short: Theorems 3.1 and 3.2 supply the derivatives appearing in the remainder.

nodes.name: Representation by induction
nodes.statement: The representation \eqref{Taylor} can be obtained by induction on $n$, using Theorem $\ref{BddnessMOI}$. See the proof of \cite[Theorem 4.1 (ii)]{CLSS} for more details.
nodes.statement_short: The multiple-operator-integral representation of the remainder follows by induction, as in CLSS.

nodes.name: Estimate
nodes.statement: From this representation, we obtain the estimate \eqref{Taylorineq} by applying Inequality \eqref{IneqDDn}.
nodes.statement_short: Applying inequality (2.9) of Theorem 2.7 to the representation gives the $\mathcal{S}^p$-bound.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.4
nodes.statement: By Theorem $\ref{FormulaSA}$, we know that $\varphi$ is $n$-times differentiable and that for any $t\in \mathbb{R}$, \begin{equation*} \dfrac{1}{n!} \varphi^{(n)}(t) = \left[ \Gamma^{A+tK, A+tK, \ldots, A+tK}(f^{[n]}) \right] (K, \ldots, K). \end{equation*} Hence, to prove the result, we have to show that the mapping $$ t \in \mathbb{R} \mapsto \left[ \Gamma^{A+tK, A+tK, \ldots, A+tK}(f^{[n]}) \right] (K, \ldots, K) \in \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H}) $$ is continuous. More generally, we will prove that for any $X = (X_1, \ldots, X_n) \in \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})^n$, the mapping $$ \varphi_X : t \in \mathbb{R} \mapsto \left[ \Gamma^{A+tK, A+tK, \ldots, A+tK}(f^{[n]}) \right] (X_1, \ldots, X_n) \in \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H}) $$ is continuous. Note that it is sufficient to prove that $\varphi_X$ is continuous in $0$. Let $h \in C^n(\mathbb{R})$. Assume that either $A$ is bounded or $h^{(i)}$ is bounded for all $1\leq i\leq n-1$ and further assume that $h^{(n)} \in C_0(\mathbb{R})$. It follows from \cite[Theorem 3.4]{LMS} that $h$ is $n$-times continuously Fr\'echet $\mathcal{S}^p$-differentiable at $A$. This implies that for any $X_1, \ldots, X_n \in \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$, the mapping \begin{equation} t\in \mathbb{R} \mapsto \left[ \Gamma^{A+tK, A+tK, \ldots, A+tK}(h^{[n]}) \right] (X_1, \ldots, X_n) \end{equation} is continuous in $0$. Hence, if $f^{(n)} \in C_0(\mathbb{R})$, $\varphi \in C^n(\mathbb{R},\Sc^p(\H))$. The rest of the proof consists in reducing to this particular case.\\ Let $(g_k)_{k\geq 1}$ be a sequence of $C^{\infty}_c(\mathbb{R})$ satisfying the following two properties: $$ \forall\, k\in\N, \quad 0\leq g_k\leq 1, \qquad\hbox{and}\qquad\forall\, r\in \mathbb{R},\quad g_k(r)\overset{k\to\infty}{\longrightarrow} 1. $$ Let $k\geq 1$. Define $G_k^n = g_k \otimes \underbrace{1 \otimes \cdots \otimes 1}_{n-1 \ \text{times}} \otimes g_k$ and write $$ G_k^n(x_1, \ldots, x_n) = h_1(x_1,x_2) h_2(x_{n-1},x_n) $$ where $h_1 = g_k \otimes 1$ and $h_2 = 1 \otimes g_k$. We have $$ \left[\Gamma^{A+tK, A+tK}(h_1)\right](X_1) = g_k(A+tK) X_1 $$ and $$\left[\Gamma^{A+tK, A+tK}(h_2)\right](X_n) = X_n g_k(A+tK). $$ Hence, by Lemma $\ref{simplification1}$, the function $$ \varphi_{k,X}^n : t \in \mathbb{R} \mapsto \left[ \Gamma^{A+tK, A+tK, \ldots, A+tK}(f^{[n]}G_k^n) \right] (X_1, \ldots, X_n) \in \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H}) $$ satisfies, for any $t\in \mathbb{R}$, $$ \varphi_{k,X}^n(t) = \left[ \Gamma^{A+tK, A+tK, \ldots, A+tK}(f^{[n]}) \right](g_k(A+tK) X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{n-1}, X_n g_k(A+tK)). $$ $(g_k)_{k\geq 1}$ is bounded and pointwise convergent to $1$ so $(g_k(A))_{k\geq 1}$ converges strongly to the identity of $\mathcal{H}$ and hence $g_k(A) X_1 \to X_1$ and $X_n g_k(A) \to X_n$ in $\mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$ as $k\to \infty$. Moreover, it follows from the arguments of the proof of \cite[Lemma 3.4]{CLSS} that $A + tK \to A$ resolvent strongly as $t \to 0$. This means that for any $u \in C_b(\mathbb{R})$, $$ u(A+tK) \underset{t \to 0}{\longrightarrow} u(A) \ \ \text{strongly}. $$ For any $k\geq 1, g_k \in C_b(\mathbb{R})$ so $g_k(A+tK) \to g_k(A)$ strongly as $t \to 0$, which implies that $g_k(A+tK) X_1 \to g_k(A) X_1$ and $X_n g_k(A+tK) \to X_n g_k(A)$ in $\mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$ as $t\to 0$. Let $\epsilon > 0$. By the latter, there exists $k_0 \in \mathbb{N}$ such that, for any $k\geq k_0$, $$ \| X_1 - g_{k_0}(A) K\|_p \leq \epsilon \ \ \text{and} \ \ \| X_n - X_n g_{k_0}(A) \|_p \leq \epsilon $$ and there exists $t_0 > 0$ such that for any $|t| \leq t_0$, $$ \| g_{k_0}(A)X_1 - g_{k_0}(A+tK) X_1\|_p \leq \epsilon \ \ \text{and} \ \ \| X_n g_{k_0}(A) - X_n g_{k_0}(A+tK) \|_p \leq \epsilon. $$ Hence, for any $|t| \leq t_0$, \begin{align*} & \| X_1 - g_{k_0}(A+tK) X_1\|_p \\ & \leq \| X_1 - g_{k_0}(A) X_1\|_p + \| g_{k_0}(A)X_1 - g_{k_0}(A+tK) X_1\|_p \\ & \leq 2 \epsilon, \end{align*} and similarly, $$ \| X_n - X_n g_{k_0}(A+tK) \|_p \leq 2\epsilon. $$ By Remark $\ref{Ineqmulti}$ and Theorem $\ref{BddnessMOI}$, there exists a constant $C > 0$ depending only on $p, n, \|f^{(n)}\|_{\infty}$ and $\|K\|_p$ such that, for any $|t| < t_0$, $$ \| \varphi_X(t) - \varphi_{k_0,X}^n(t) \|_p \leq C \epsilon. $$ By the triangle inequality we get that for any $|t| < t_0$, \begin{align*} & \| \varphi_X(t) - \varphi_X(0) \|_p \\ & \leq \| \varphi_X(t) - \varphi_{k_0,X}^n(t) \|_p + \|\varphi_{k_0,X}^n(t) - \varphi_{k_0,X}^n(0) \|_p + \| \varphi_{k_0,X}^n(0) - \varphi_X(0)\|_p \\ & \leq 2C \epsilon + \|\varphi_{k_0,X}^n(t) - \varphi_{k_0,X}^n(0) \|_p. \end{align*} Hence, to prove the result, it suffices to prove that for any $k\geq 1$ and any $X \in \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})^n, \varphi_{k,X}^n$ is continuous in $0$.\\ Fix $k\geq 1$ and let $g = g_k$. We will prove the continuity of $\varphi_{k,X}^n$ in $0$ by induction on $n$. For $n=1$, we have, for any $(x_0,x_1)\in \mathbb{R}^2$ with $x_0 \neq x_1$, \begin{align} \begin{split} f^{[1]}(x_0,x_1)g(x_0)g(x_1) & = \dfrac{g(x_1)(gf)(x_0) - (gf)(x_1) g(x_0)}{x_0 - x_1} \\ & = \dfrac{g(x_1)(gf)(x_0) - g(x_1)(gf)(x_1)}{x_0 - x_1} \\ & \ \ \ \ + \dfrac{(gf)(x_1)g(x_1) - (gf)(x_1) g(x_0)}{x_0 - x_1} \\ & = g(x_1) (gf)^{[1]}(x_0,x_1) - (gf)(x_1)g^{[1]}(x_0,x_1). \end{split} \end{align} By continuity, this equality holds true for any $x_0,x_1 \in \mathbb{R}$. Hence, by Lemma $\ref{simplification1}$, we have, for any $t\in \mathbb{R}$ and any $X\in \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$, \begin{align*} & \varphi_{k,X}^1(t) \\ & = \left[ \Gamma^{A+tK, A+tK}((gf)^{[1]}) \right](Xg(A+tK)) - \left[ \Gamma^{A+tK, A+tK}(g^{[1]}) \right](X(gf)(A+tK)). \end{align*} As explained in the first part of the proof, the mappings $t\in \mathbb{R} \mapsto Xg(A+tK) \in \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$ and $t\in \mathbb{R} \mapsto X(gf)(A+tK) \in \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$ are continuous in $0$. Note that $g', (gf)' \in C_0(\mathbb{R})$ so that, by continuity of the map defined in \eqref{casefnC0} and the uniform boundedness of the mappings $\Gamma^{A+tK, A+tK}((gf)^{[1]}), \Gamma^{A+tK, A+tK}(g^{[1]}), t\in \mathbb{R}$, we get that \begin{align*} \underset{t\to 0}{\lim} ~ \varphi_{k,X}^1(t) = \left[ \Gamma^{A, A}((gf)^{[1]}) \right](Xg(A)) - \left[ \Gamma^{A, A}(g^{[1]}) \right](X(gf)(A)) = \varphi_{k,X}^1(0), \end{align*} so that $\varphi_{k,X}^1$ is continuous in $0$. Now, let $n\geq 2$ and assume that for any $1\leq i \leq n-1$ and any $X=(X_1,\ldots, X_{i}) \in \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})^i$, $\varphi_{k,X}^{i}$ is continuous in $0$. First, we show by induction the following formula: for every $(x_0,\ldots,x_n) \in \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$, \begin{align} \begin{split} & f^{[n]}(x_0, \ldots, x_n)g(x_0) \\ & = (gf)^{[n]}(x_0, \ldots, x_n) - f(x_n) g^{[n]}(x_0,\ldots, x_n) - \sum_{l=1}^{n-1} g^{[l]}(x_0, \ldots, x_l)f^{[n-l]}(x_{l} ,\ldots, x_n). \end{split} \end{align} For $n=2$, first note that the computations made in \eqref{calculsn1} give $$ f^{[1]}(x_0,x_1)g(x_0) = (gf)^{[1]}(x_0,x_1) - f(x_1)g^{[1]}(x_0,x_1) $$ so that \begin{align*} & f^{[2]}(x_0,x_1,x_2)g(x_0) \\ & = \dfrac{f^{[1]}(x_0,x_2)g(x_0) - f^{[1]}(x_1,x_2)g(x_1)}{x_0-x_1} + \dfrac{f^{[1]}(x_1,x_2)g(x_1) - f^{[1]}(x_1,x_2)g(x_0)}{x_0-x_1} \\ & = \dfrac{(gf)^{[1]}(x_0,x_2) - f(x_2)g^{[1]}(x_0,x_2) - (gf)^{[1]}(x_1,x_2) + f(x_2)g^{[1]}(x_1,x_2)}{x_0-x_1} \\ & \ \ \ \ - g^{[1]}(x_0,x_1)f^{[1]}(x_1,x_2) \\ & = (gf)^{[2]}(x_0,x_1,x_2) - f(x_2) g^{[2]}(x_0,x_1,x_2) - g^{[1]}(x_0,x_1)f^{[1]}(x_1,x_2), \end{align*} which shows \eqref{recfng} for $n=2$. Assume now that we have \eqref{recfng} at the order $n$ and show that it still holds true at the order $n+1$. We have \begin{align} \begin{split} & f^{[n+1]}(x_0,\ldots, x_{n+1})g(x_0) \\ & = \dfrac{f^{[n]}(x_0, x_2, \ldots, x_{n+1})g(x_0) - f^{[n]}(x_1,\ldots, x_{n+1})g(x_1)}{x_0-x_1} \\ & \ \ \ \ + \dfrac{f^{[n]}(x_1,\ldots, x_{n+1})g(x_1) - f^{[n]}(x_1,\ldots, x_{n+1})g(x_0)}{x_0-x_1} \\ & = \dfrac{f^{[n]}(x_0, x_2, \ldots, x_{n+1})g(x_0) - f^{[n]}(x_1,\ldots, x_{n+1})g(x_1)}{x_0-x_1} \\ & \ \ \ \ - g^{[1]}(x_0,x_1) f^{[n]}(x_1,\ldots, x_{n+1}). \end{split} \end{align} By assumption, we have \begin{align} \begin{split} & \dfrac{f^{[n]}(x_0, x_2, \ldots, x_{n+1})g(x_0) - f^{[n]}(x_1,\ldots, x_{n+1})g(x_1)}{x_0-x_1} \\ & = \dfrac{(gf)^{[n]}(x_0, x_2, \ldots, x_{n+1}) - (gf)^{[n]}(x_1, \ldots, x_{n+1})}{x_0-x_1} \\ & \ \ \ \ - f(x_{n+1}) \dfrac{g^{[n]}(x_0,x_2,\ldots, x_{n+1}) - g^{[n]}(x_1,\ldots, x_{n+1})}{x_0-x_1} \\ & \ \ \ \ - \sum_{l=1}^{n-1} \dfrac{g^{[l]}(x_0,x_2, \ldots, x_{l+1})-g^{[l]}(x_1, \ldots, x_{l+1})}{x_0-x_1}f^{[n-l]}(x_{l+1} ,\ldots, x_{n+1}) \\ & = (gf)^{[n+1]}(x_0, \ldots, x_{n+1}) - f(x_{n+1}) g^{[n+1]}(x_0,\ldots, x_{n+1}) \\ & \ \ \ \ - \sum_{l=1}^{n-1} g^{[l+1]}(x_0, \ldots, x_{l+1}) f^{[n-l]}(x_{l+1} ,\ldots, x_{n+1}). \end{split} \end{align} We have \begin{align*} & \sum_{l=1}^{n-1} g^{[l+1]}(x_0, \ldots, x_{l+1}) f^{[n-l]}(x_{l+1} ,\ldots, x_{n+1}) + g^{[1]}(x_0,x_1) f^{[n]}(x_1,\ldots, x_{n+1}) \\ & = \sum_{j=2}^{n} g^{[j]}(x_0, \ldots, x_j) f^{[n+1-j]}(x_j ,\ldots, x_{n+1}) + g^{[1]}(x_0,x_1) f^{[n]}(x_1,\ldots, x_{n+1}) \\ & = \sum_{j=1}^{n} g^{[j]}(x_0, \ldots, x_j) f^{[n+1-j]}(x_j ,\ldots, x_{n+1}). \end{align*} Hence, by \eqref{recu1} and \eqref{recu2}, Formula \eqref{recfng} is proved at the order $n+1$. Note that the previous computations make sense when $x_0 \neq x_1$ and by continuity, the formula also holds true for $x_0 = x_1$. Let $(x_0, \ldots, x_n)\in \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$. We multiply Formula \eqref{recfng} by $g(x_n)$ and we get \begin{align*} f^{[n]}G_k^n(x_0, \ldots, x_n) & = g(x_n)(gf)^{[n]}(x_0, \ldots, x_n) - (gf)(x_n) g^{[n]}(x_0,\ldots, x_n) \\ & \ \ \ - g(x_n)\sum_{l=1}^{n-1} g^{[l]}(x_0, \ldots, x_l)f^{[n-l]}(x_{l} ,\ldots, x_n). \end{align*} Let $X_1, \ldots, X_n \in \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$. Applying the operator $$ \left[\Gamma^{A+tK, \ldots, A+tK}(\cdot)\right](X_1,\ldots, X_n) $$ to the previous equality gives, by Lemma $\ref{simplification1}$ and Lemma $\ref{simplificationsep}$, \begin{align*} \varphi_{k,X}^n(t) = \varphi_1(t) - \varphi_2(t) - \sum_{l=1}^{n-1} \varphi_{3,l}(t) \end{align*} where $$ \varphi_1(t) = \left[\Gamma^{A+tK, \ldots, A+tK}((gf)^{[n]})\right](X_1,\ldots, X_{n-1}, X_ng(A+tK)), $$ $$ \varphi_2(t) = \left[\Gamma^{A+tK, \ldots, A+tK}(g^{[n]})\right](X_1,\ldots, X_{n-1}, X_n (gf)(A+tK)), $$ and for any $1\leq l \leq n-1$, $$ \varphi_{3,l}(t) = \varphi_{3,l}^1(t)\varphi_{3,l}^2(t) $$ with $$ \varphi_{3,l}^1(t) = \left[\Gamma^{A+tK, \ldots, A+tK}(g^{[l]})\right](X_1,\ldots,X_{l}) $$ and $$\varphi_{3,l}^2(t) = \left[\Gamma^{A+tK, \ldots, A+tK}(f^{[n-l]})\right](X_{l+1},\ldots, X_{n-1}, X_n g(A+tK)). $$ The functions $g$ and $gf$ belong to $C_b(\mathbb{R})$ so the mappings $t \in \mathbb{R} \mapsto X_ng(A+tK) \in \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$ and $t \in \mathbb{R} \mapsto X_n (gf)(A+tK) \in \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$ are continuous in $0$. We have $(gf)^{(n)}, g^{(n)} \in C_0(\mathbb{R})$ so by the continuity of the map defined in \eqref{casefnC0}, we get that $\varphi_1$ and $\varphi_2$ are continuous in $0$. Now let $1 \leq l \leq n-1$. Since $g^{(l)} \in C_0(\mathbb{R})$, $\varphi_{3,l}^1$ is continuous in $0$. We have $1 \leq n-l \leq n-1$, and by assumption, $\varphi_{k,Y}^{n-l}$ is continuous in $0$ for any $Y \in \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})^l$. Hence, by composition with the continuous map $t \in \mathbb{R} \mapsto X_ng(A+tK) \in \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$, we get that $\varphi_{3,l}^2$ is continuous in $0$, so that $\varphi_{3,l}$ also is. We hence proved that $\varphi_{k,X}$ is continuous in $0$, which concludes the proof of the proposition.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce continuity of $t\mapsto[\Gamma^{A+tK,\ldots}(f^{[n]})](X)$ to symbols cut off by $G_k^n$, then prove continuity of $\varphi^n_{k,X}$ by induction on $n$ using the divided-difference identity for $f^{[n]}g$.

nodes.name: Reduce to continuity of the $n$th derivative
nodes.statement: By Theorem $\ref{FormulaSA}$, we know that $\varphi$ is $n$-times differentiable and that for any $t\in \mathbb{R}$, \begin{equation*} \dfrac{1}{n!} \varphi^{(n)}(t) = \left[ \Gamma^{A+tK, A+tK, \ldots, A+tK}(f^{[n]}) \right] (K, \ldots, K). \end{equation*} Hence, to prove the result, we have to show that the mapping $$ t \in \mathbb{R} \mapsto \left[ \Gamma^{A+tK, A+tK, \ldots, A+tK}(f^{[n]}) \right] (K, \ldots, K) \in \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H}) $$ is continuous.
nodes.statement_short: By Theorem 3.1 only continuity of $t\mapsto[\Gamma^{A+tK,\ldots}(f^{[n]})](K,\ldots,K)$ remains.

nodes.name: Generalise to arbitrary arguments
nodes.statement: More generally, we will prove that for any $X = (X_1, \ldots, X_n) \in \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})^n$, the mapping $$ \varphi_X : t \in \mathbb{R} \mapsto \left[ \Gamma^{A+tK, A+tK, \ldots, A+tK}(f^{[n]}) \right] (X_1, \ldots, X_n) \in \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H}) $$ is continuous. Note that it is sufficient to prove that $\varphi_X$ is continuous in $0$.
nodes.statement_short: Prove continuity at $0$ of $\varphi_X$ for arbitrary $X\in(\mathcal{S}^p)^n$.

nodes.name: The case $f^{(n)}\in C_0$
nodes.statement: Let $h \in C^n(\mathbb{R})$. Assume that either $A$ is bounded or $h^{(i)}$ is bounded for all $1\leq i\leq n-1$ and further assume that $h^{(n)} \in C_0(\mathbb{R})$. It follows from \cite[Theorem 3.4]{LMS} that $h$ is $n$-times continuously Fr\'echet $\mathcal{S}^p$-differentiable at $A$. This implies that for any $X_1, \ldots, X_n \in \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$, the mapping \begin{equation} t\in \mathbb{R} \mapsto \left[ \Gamma^{A+tK, A+tK, \ldots, A+tK}(h^{[n]}) \right] (X_1, \ldots, X_n) \end{equation} is continuous in $0$. Hence, if $f^{(n)} \in C_0(\mathbb{R})$, $\varphi \in C^n(\mathbb{R},\Sc^p(\H))$. The rest of the proof consists in reducing to this particular case.\\
nodes.statement_short: For $h^{(n)}\in C_0(\mathbb{R})$, LMS gives $n$-times continuous Frechet differentiability, hence continuity of the map.

nodes.name: Cut-off symbols $G_k^n$
nodes.statement: Let $(g_k)_{k\geq 1}$ be a sequence of $C^{\infty}_c(\mathbb{R})$ satisfying the following two properties: $$ \forall\, k\in\N, \quad 0\leq g_k\leq 1, \qquad\hbox{and}\qquad\forall\, r\in \mathbb{R},\quad g_k(r)\overset{k\to\infty}{\longrightarrow} 1. $$ Let $k\geq 1$. Define $G_k^n = g_k \otimes \underbrace{1 \otimes \cdots \otimes 1}_{n-1 \ \text{times}} \otimes g_k$ and write $$ G_k^n(x_1, \ldots, x_n) = h_1(x_1,x_2) h_2(x_{n-1},x_n) $$ where $h_1 = g_k \otimes 1$ and $h_2 = 1 \otimes g_k$. We have $$ \left[\Gamma^{A+tK, A+tK}(h_1)\right](X_1) = g_k(A+tK) X_1 $$ and $$\left[\Gamma^{A+tK, A+tK}(h_2)\right](X_n) = X_n g_k(A+tK). $$ Hence, by Lemma $\ref{simplification1}$, the function $$ \varphi_{k,X}^n : t \in \mathbb{R} \mapsto \left[ \Gamma^{A+tK, A+tK, \ldots, A+tK}(f^{[n]}G_k^n) \right] (X_1, \ldots, X_n) \in \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H}) $$ satisfies, for any $t\in \mathbb{R}$, $$ \varphi_{k,X}^n(t) = \left[ \Gamma^{A+tK, A+tK, \ldots, A+tK}(f^{[n]}) \right](g_k(A+tK) X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_{n-1}, X_n g_k(A+tK)). $$
nodes.statement_short: Introduce $G_k^n=g_k\otimes1\otimes\cdots\otimes1\otimes g_k$ and use Lemma 2.4 to move the cut-offs onto $X_1$ and $X_n$.

nodes.name: Strong convergence of $g_k(A+tK)$
nodes.statement: $(g_k)_{k\geq 1}$ is bounded and pointwise convergent to $1$ so $(g_k(A))_{k\geq 1}$ converges strongly to the identity of $\mathcal{H}$ and hence $g_k(A) X_1 \to X_1$ and $X_n g_k(A) \to X_n$ in $\mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$ as $k\to \infty$. Moreover, it follows from the arguments of the proof of \cite[Lemma 3.4]{CLSS} that $A + tK \to A$ resolvent strongly as $t \to 0$. This means that for any $u \in C_b(\mathbb{R})$, $$ u(A+tK) \underset{t \to 0}{\longrightarrow} u(A) \ \ \text{strongly}. $$ For any $k\geq 1, g_k \in C_b(\mathbb{R})$ so $g_k(A+tK) \to g_k(A)$ strongly as $t \to 0$, which implies that $g_k(A+tK) X_1 \to g_k(A) X_1$ and $X_n g_k(A+tK) \to X_n g_k(A)$ in $\mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$ as $t\to 0$.
nodes.statement_short: $g_k(A)\to1$ strongly and $A+tK\to A$ in the resolvent sense, so $g_k(A+tK)X_1\to g_k(A)X_1$.

nodes.name: Uniform approximation of $\varphi_X$ by $\varphi^n_{k_0,X}$
nodes.statement: Let $\epsilon > 0$. By the latter, there exists $k_0 \in \mathbb{N}$ such that, for any $k\geq k_0$, $$ \| X_1 - g_{k_0}(A) K\|_p \leq \epsilon \ \ \text{and} \ \ \| X_n - X_n g_{k_0}(A) \|_p \leq \epsilon $$ and there exists $t_0 > 0$ such that for any $|t| \leq t_0$, $$ \| g_{k_0}(A)X_1 - g_{k_0}(A+tK) X_1\|_p \leq \epsilon \ \ \text{and} \ \ \| X_n g_{k_0}(A) - X_n g_{k_0}(A+tK) \|_p \leq \epsilon. $$ Hence, for any $|t| \leq t_0$, \begin{align*} & \| X_1 - g_{k_0}(A+tK) X_1\|_p \\ & \leq \| X_1 - g_{k_0}(A) X_1\|_p + \| g_{k_0}(A)X_1 - g_{k_0}(A+tK) X_1\|_p \\ & \leq 2 \epsilon, \end{align*} and similarly, $$ \| X_n - X_n g_{k_0}(A+tK) \|_p \leq 2\epsilon. $$ By Remark $\ref{Ineqmulti}$ and Theorem $\ref{BddnessMOI}$, there exists a constant $C > 0$ depending only on $p, n, \|f^{(n)}\|_{\infty}$ and $\|K\|_p$ such that, for any $|t| < t_0$, $$ \| \varphi_X(t) - \varphi_{k_0,X}^n(t) \|_p \leq C \epsilon. $$
nodes.statement_short: Choose $k_0$ and $t_0$ so that the cut-off arguments are $2\epsilon$-close, then apply Remark 2.2 and Theorem 2.7.

nodes.name: Reduce to continuity of $\varphi^n_{k,X}$
nodes.statement: By the triangle inequality we get that for any $|t| < t_0$, \begin{align*} & \| \varphi_X(t) - \varphi_X(0) \|_p \\ & \leq \| \varphi_X(t) - \varphi_{k_0,X}^n(t) \|_p + \|\varphi_{k_0,X}^n(t) - \varphi_{k_0,X}^n(0) \|_p + \| \varphi_{k_0,X}^n(0) - \varphi_X(0)\|_p \\ & \leq 2C \epsilon + \|\varphi_{k_0,X}^n(t) - \varphi_{k_0,X}^n(0) \|_p. \end{align*} Hence, to prove the result, it suffices to prove that for any $k\geq 1$ and any $X \in \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})^n, \varphi_{k,X}^n$ is continuous in $0$.\\
nodes.statement_short: The triangle inequality shows it suffices to prove each $\varphi^n_{k,X}$ is continuous at $0$.

nodes.name: Induction base $n=1$
nodes.statement: Fix $k\geq 1$ and let $g = g_k$. We will prove the continuity of $\varphi_{k,X}^n$ in $0$ by induction on $n$. For $n=1$, we have, for any $(x_0,x_1)\in \mathbb{R}^2$ with $x_0 \neq x_1$, \begin{align} \begin{split} f^{[1]}(x_0,x_1)g(x_0)g(x_1) & = \dfrac{g(x_1)(gf)(x_0) - (gf)(x_1) g(x_0)}{x_0 - x_1} \\ & = \dfrac{g(x_1)(gf)(x_0) - g(x_1)(gf)(x_1)}{x_0 - x_1} \\ & \ \ \ \ + \dfrac{(gf)(x_1)g(x_1) - (gf)(x_1) g(x_0)}{x_0 - x_1} \\ & = g(x_1) (gf)^{[1]}(x_0,x_1) - (gf)(x_1)g^{[1]}(x_0,x_1). \end{split} \end{align} By continuity, this equality holds true for any $x_0,x_1 \in \mathbb{R}$. Hence, by Lemma $\ref{simplification1}$, we have, for any $t\in \mathbb{R}$ and any $X\in \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$, \begin{align*} & \varphi_{k,X}^1(t) \\ & = \left[ \Gamma^{A+tK, A+tK}((gf)^{[1]}) \right](Xg(A+tK)) - \left[ \Gamma^{A+tK, A+tK}(g^{[1]}) \right](X(gf)(A+tK)). \end{align*} As explained in the first part of the proof, the mappings $t\in \mathbb{R} \mapsto Xg(A+tK) \in \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$ and $t\in \mathbb{R} \mapsto X(gf)(A+tK) \in \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$ are continuous in $0$. Note that $g', (gf)' \in C_0(\mathbb{R})$ so that, by continuity of the map defined in \eqref{casefnC0} and the uniform boundedness of the mappings $\Gamma^{A+tK, A+tK}((gf)^{[1]}), \Gamma^{A+tK, A+tK}(g^{[1]}), t\in \mathbb{R}$, we get that \begin{align*} \underset{t\to 0}{\lim} ~ \varphi_{k,X}^1(t) = \left[ \Gamma^{A, A}((gf)^{[1]}) \right](Xg(A)) - \left[ \Gamma^{A, A}(g^{[1]}) \right](X(gf)(A)) = \varphi_{k,X}^1(0), \end{align*} so that $\varphi_{k,X}^1$ is continuous in $0$.
nodes.statement_short: For $n=1$ the identity $f^{[1]}gg=g(gf)^{[1]}-(gf)g^{[1]}$ plus Lemma 2.4 gives continuity.

nodes.name: Induction hypothesis and the symbol formula
nodes.statement: Now, let $n\geq 2$ and assume that for any $1\leq i \leq n-1$ and any $X=(X_1,\ldots, X_{i}) \in \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})^i$, $\varphi_{k,X}^{i}$ is continuous in $0$. First, we show by induction the following formula: for every $(x_0,\ldots,x_n) \in \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$, \begin{align} \begin{split} & f^{[n]}(x_0, \ldots, x_n)g(x_0) \\ & = (gf)^{[n]}(x_0, \ldots, x_n) - f(x_n) g^{[n]}(x_0,\ldots, x_n) - \sum_{l=1}^{n-1} g^{[l]}(x_0, \ldots, x_l)f^{[n-l]}(x_{l} ,\ldots, x_n). \end{split} \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Assume continuity in lower orders and state the formula for $f^{[n]}(x)g(x_0)$.

nodes.name: Formula at order $2$
nodes.statement_short: Verify the symbol formula for $n=2$ by direct computation.

nodes.name: Induction step for the symbol formula
nodes.statement: Assume now that we have \eqref{recfng} at the order $n$ and show that it still holds true at the order $n+1$. We have \begin{align} \begin{split} & f^{[n+1]}(x_0,\ldots, x_{n+1})g(x_0) \\ & = \dfrac{f^{[n]}(x_0, x_2, \ldots, x_{n+1})g(x_0) - f^{[n]}(x_1,\ldots, x_{n+1})g(x_1)}{x_0-x_1} \\ & \ \ \ \ + \dfrac{f^{[n]}(x_1,\ldots, x_{n+1})g(x_1) - f^{[n]}(x_1,\ldots, x_{n+1})g(x_0)}{x_0-x_1} \\ & = \dfrac{f^{[n]}(x_0, x_2, \ldots, x_{n+1})g(x_0) - f^{[n]}(x_1,\ldots, x_{n+1})g(x_1)}{x_0-x_1} \\ & \ \ \ \ - g^{[1]}(x_0,x_1) f^{[n]}(x_1,\ldots, x_{n+1}). \end{split} \end{align} By assumption, we have \begin{align} \begin{split} & \dfrac{f^{[n]}(x_0, x_2, \ldots, x_{n+1})g(x_0) - f^{[n]}(x_1,\ldots, x_{n+1})g(x_1)}{x_0-x_1} \\ & = \dfrac{(gf)^{[n]}(x_0, x_2, \ldots, x_{n+1}) - (gf)^{[n]}(x_1, \ldots, x_{n+1})}{x_0-x_1} \\ & \ \ \ \ - f(x_{n+1}) \dfrac{g^{[n]}(x_0,x_2,\ldots, x_{n+1}) - g^{[n]}(x_1,\ldots, x_{n+1})}{x_0-x_1} \\ & \ \ \ \ - \sum_{l=1}^{n-1} \dfrac{g^{[l]}(x_0,x_2, \ldots, x_{l+1})-g^{[l]}(x_1, \ldots, x_{l+1})}{x_0-x_1}f^{[n-l]}(x_{l+1} ,\ldots, x_{n+1}) \\ & = (gf)^{[n+1]}(x_0, \ldots, x_{n+1}) - f(x_{n+1}) g^{[n+1]}(x_0,\ldots, x_{n+1}) \\ & \ \ \ \ - \sum_{l=1}^{n-1} g^{[l+1]}(x_0, \ldots, x_{l+1}) f^{[n-l]}(x_{l+1} ,\ldots, x_{n+1}). \end{split} \end{align} We have \begin{align*} & \sum_{l=1}^{n-1} g^{[l+1]}(x_0, \ldots, x_{l+1}) f^{[n-l]}(x_{l+1} ,\ldots, x_{n+1}) + g^{[1]}(x_0,x_1) f^{[n]}(x_1,\ldots, x_{n+1}) \\ & = \sum_{j=2}^{n} g^{[j]}(x_0, \ldots, x_j) f^{[n+1-j]}(x_j ,\ldots, x_{n+1}) + g^{[1]}(x_0,x_1) f^{[n]}(x_1,\ldots, x_{n+1}) \\ & = \sum_{j=1}^{n} g^{[j]}(x_0, \ldots, x_j) f^{[n+1-j]}(x_j ,\ldots, x_{n+1}). \end{align*} Hence, by \eqref{recu1} and \eqref{recu2}, Formula \eqref{recfng} is proved at the order $n+1$.
nodes.statement_short: Pass from order $n$ to order $n+1$ by expanding the difference quotients and re-indexing the sum.

nodes.name: Multiply by $g(x_n)$
nodes.statement: Note that the previous computations make sense when $x_0 \neq x_1$ and by continuity, the formula also holds true for $x_0 = x_1$. Let $(x_0, \ldots, x_n)\in \mathbb{R}^{n+1}$. We multiply Formula \eqref{recfng} by $g(x_n)$ and we get \begin{align*} f^{[n]}G_k^n(x_0, \ldots, x_n) & = g(x_n)(gf)^{[n]}(x_0, \ldots, x_n) - (gf)(x_n) g^{[n]}(x_0,\ldots, x_n) \\ & \ \ \ - g(x_n)\sum_{l=1}^{n-1} g^{[l]}(x_0, \ldots, x_l)f^{[n-l]}(x_{l} ,\ldots, x_n). \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Continuity extends the formula to the diagonal; multiplying by $g(x_n)$ gives the expansion of $f^{[n]}G_k^n$.

nodes.name: Split $\varphi^n_{k,X}$ into three families
nodes.statement: Let $X_1, \ldots, X_n \in \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$. Applying the operator $$ \left[\Gamma^{A+tK, \ldots, A+tK}(\cdot)\right](X_1,\ldots, X_n) $$ to the previous equality gives, by Lemma $\ref{simplification1}$ and Lemma $\ref{simplificationsep}$, \begin{align*} \varphi_{k,X}^n(t) = \varphi_1(t) - \varphi_2(t) - \sum_{l=1}^{n-1} \varphi_{3,l}(t) \end{align*} where $$ \varphi_1(t) = \left[\Gamma^{A+tK, \ldots, A+tK}((gf)^{[n]})\right](X_1,\ldots, X_{n-1}, X_ng(A+tK)), $$ $$ \varphi_2(t) = \left[\Gamma^{A+tK, \ldots, A+tK}(g^{[n]})\right](X_1,\ldots, X_{n-1}, X_n (gf)(A+tK)), $$ and for any $1\leq l \leq n-1$, $$ \varphi_{3,l}(t) = \varphi_{3,l}^1(t)\varphi_{3,l}^2(t) $$ with $$ \varphi_{3,l}^1(t) = \left[\Gamma^{A+tK, \ldots, A+tK}(g^{[l]})\right](X_1,\ldots,X_{l}) $$ and $$\varphi_{3,l}^2(t) = \left[\Gamma^{A+tK, \ldots, A+tK}(f^{[n-l]})\right](X_{l+1},\ldots, X_{n-1}, X_n g(A+tK)). $$
nodes.statement_short: Lemmas 2.4 and 2.5 turn the symbol expansion into $\varphi_1-\varphi_2-\sum_l\varphi_{3,l}$.

nodes.name: Continuity of $\varphi_1$ and $\varphi_2$
nodes.statement: The functions $g$ and $gf$ belong to $C_b(\mathbb{R})$ so the mappings $t \in \mathbb{R} \mapsto X_ng(A+tK) \in \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$ and $t \in \mathbb{R} \mapsto X_n (gf)(A+tK) \in \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$ are continuous in $0$. We have $(gf)^{(n)}, g^{(n)} \in C_0(\mathbb{R})$ so by the continuity of the map defined in \eqref{casefnC0}, we get that $\varphi_1$ and $\varphi_2$ are continuous in $0$.
nodes.statement_short: $(gf)^{(n)},g^{(n)}\in C_0(\mathbb{R})$, so the $C_0$ case applies.

nodes.name: Continuity of the $\varphi_{3,l}$ and conclusion
nodes.statement: Now let $1 \leq l \leq n-1$. Since $g^{(l)} \in C_0(\mathbb{R})$, $\varphi_{3,l}^1$ is continuous in $0$. We have $1 \leq n-l \leq n-1$, and by assumption, $\varphi_{k,Y}^{n-l}$ is continuous in $0$ for any $Y \in \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})^l$. Hence, by composition with the continuous map $t \in \mathbb{R} \mapsto X_ng(A+tK) \in \mathcal{S}^p(\mathcal{H})$, we get that $\varphi_{3,l}^2$ is continuous in $0$, so that $\varphi_{3,l}$ also is. We hence proved that $\varphi_{k,X}$ is continuous in $0$, which concludes the proof of the proposition.
nodes.statement_short: The first factor is continuous by the $C_0$ case and the second by the induction hypothesis, finishing the proof.
